findings.detail: Collection Fund monitoring forecasts £646k deficit impact split between £52k taxbase shortfall (34 Band D properties) and £593k increased bad debt provision requirement. The council also carries £22m in outstanding historic council tax debt with only £16m bad debt provision coverage. These indicators suggest collection challenges.
findings.matters: Collection deterioration is often an early indicator of resident economic stress; a lender needs to track whether this is local to Hillingdon or sector-wide
findings.figures: £646k collection fund deficit forecast; £22m outstanding historic debt; £593k additional bad debt provision needed
findings.quote: In total, these two forecasts would mount to £646k – which would impact as a pressure in 2026/27.

findings.paper_title: REPORT BM - M2 - 2026
findings.headline: 39% of planned 2026/27 savings (approximately £10.5m) remain at risk or deferred
findings.detail: Of £27.1m in combined new and rolled-forward savings being monitored, only 61% is delivered or on track (33% delivered, 28% on track). The remaining 39% is either at risk or deferred to future years. The council notes this is an improvement on prior year (41% last year) but still represents material delivery risk.
findings.matters: Current reported £584k overspend assumes all remaining at-risk savings eventually deliver; if these fail, the position deteriorates by approximately £10.5m against the £10m contingency buffer
findings.figures: 61% delivered or on track; 39% at risk or deferred; £27.1m total savings being monitored
findings.quote: Progress on delivering agreed savings is also improved on the previous financial year at this stage of the financial year, with 61% identified as delivered or on track (compared to 41% last year).

findings.paper_title: REPORT BM - M2 - 2026
findings.headline: Previously approved capital scheme (Water Sports Facility) cancelled with £6.974m budget withdrawal
findings.detail: Cabinet approved capital roll-forward of £22.872m in June 2026, but this report now declares £6.974m of that unneeded relating to the Water Sports Facility. This represents a material mid-year reversal of capital plans and signals either budget constraints forcing reprioritisation or delivery problems with the scheme.
findings.matters: A lender assessing capital discipline and budget forecast reliability needs to understand whether major schemes routinely shift or whether this is exceptional
findings.figures: £6.974m previously approved roll-forward now unneeded
findings.quote: £6.974m of that previously approved Roll-Forward is now deemed unneeded relating to the Hillingdon Water Sports Facility.

findings.paper_title: REPORT BM - M2 - 2026
findings.headline: Adult services demand overspends are structural and explicitly flagged as continuing into 2027/28 budget
findings.detail: SEN transport demand is £273k over budget and client care numbers are running 61 greater than assumed (£923k overspend). The council explicitly warns these issues will continue and will create additional unbudgeted pressure in the 2027/28 MTFS. This signals ahead-of-curve budget amendment will be needed.
findings.matters: A lender assessing medium-term sustainability needs to see whether the council's MTFS already accounts for these pressures or whether they represent unplanned growth
findings.figures: £273k SEN transport overspend; £923k client care numbers overspend; 61 additional clients vs budget
findings.quote: These issues are expected to continue into 2027/28 and will be an additional unbudgeted pressure in the 2027/28 Medium-Term Financial Strategy [MTFS].

findings.paper_title: REPORT BM - M2 - 2026
findings.headline: DSG deficit has grown to £10.6m and continues to accumulate despite statutory relief
findings.detail: The Dedicated Schools Grant deficit is forecast to overspend by £10.6m in 2026/27. While a statutory override allows this to be transferred to a negative reserve, this represents a material and growing liability driven by surge in SEND applications following government policy changes. The mechanism masks but does not eliminate the cash pressure.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand whether SEND pressures will eventually require council reserves or borrowing to resolve, or whether government policy will eventually fund the liability properly
findings.figures: £10.6m DSG overspend forecast
findings.quote: changes announced by government to the Special Education and Need Disability [SEND] system have seen a significant surge in applications. As a result, the DSG deficit is expected to overspend by £10.6m in the current year.

findings.paper_title: Consideration of setting a licensed deficit budget for schools in the Borough 2026/27
findings.paper_url: https://modgov.hillingdon.gov.uk/documents/s67257/10 - REPORT DRAFT Consideration of Setting a Licensed Deficit Budget in 2026-27 for a number of scho.pdf
findings.headline: Most school recovery plans depend on pupil roll growth that contradicts recent trends of declining birth rates
findings.detail: Multiple schools project return to surplus based on assumed pupil roll growth. However, Frithwood's roll declined from 428 (2020/21) to 352 (2026/27); Whiteheath Junior fell from 337 (2023/24) to 301 (2025/26); Harlyn expects Reception admissions at 'approximately one-form entry level.' The paper identifies 'a sustained fall in pupil numbers, linked to local birth rate decline' as a primary driver. If birth rates continue declining and pupil rolls do not recover as assumed, deficits will worsen and cash support requirements will increase.
findings.matters: The credibility of all 10 recovery plans rests on assumptions about future pupil numbers. If these prove wrong, the council faces a material risk of cascading deficits and further cash drain.
findings.figures: Frithwood roll decline from 428 to 352 over 6 years; Whiteheath decline from 337 to 301 over 2 years; local birth rate decline cited as principal driver
findings.quote: falling rolls have progressively reduced the school's income

findings.paper_title: Consideration of setting a licensed deficit budget for schools in the Borough 2026/27
findings.paper_url: https://modgov.hillingdon.gov.uk/documents/s67257/10 - REPORT DRAFT Consideration of Setting a Licensed Deficit Budget in 2026-27 for a number of scho.pdf
findings.headline: Harlyn Primary School deficit deteriorating sharply: projected to worsen from £459k to £988k by 2028/29 despite recovery plan
findings.detail: Harlyn's deficit swung from £137k in 2025/26 to a projected £459k in 2026/27, driven by an in-year shortfall of £321k. The three-year forecast shows deficits continuing to deepen: £754k in 2027/28 and £988k in 2028/29. The paper explicitly states 'the planned savings, whilst meaningful, are insufficient to offset the structural income shortfall.' As a result, Harlyn is flagged as subject to heightened local authority monitoring with requirement for a revised recovery plan, indicating the current plan is not deemed credible.
findings.matters: A deteriorating deficit that worsens despite recovery measures signals either the plan is unachievable or further structural intervention (like delegation withdrawal or closure) may be needed. This is a higher-risk case than the others.
findings.figures: Harlyn 2025/26 closing balance -£137,667; 2026/27 in-year movement -£321,755; projected 2028/29 deficit £988k
findings.quote: the planned savings, whilst meaningful, are insufficient to offset the structural income shortfall, and further action will be required to return the school to a sustainable position.

findings.paper_url: https://modgov.hillingdon.gov.uk/documents/s67257/10 - REPORT DRAFT Consideration of Setting a Licensed Deficit Budget in 2026-27 for a number of scho.pdf
findings.headline: Hillingdon schools hold £4.2m accumulated deficit with £2.5m+ in outstanding council loans, largest concentration in one secondary school
findings.detail: Ten schools are licensed to run deficits totalling £4,224,264 accumulated as of end 2025/26. findings.figures: Total accumulated deficit £4,224,264; Oak Wood £2.627m deficit with £2.5m outstanding loan; in-year movements ranging from -£322k (Harlyn) to +£81k (Lady Bankes) in 2026/27

findings.paper_title: Provisional Audit Planning Report , item 17.
findings.headline: Significant property valuations (£833.7m land and buildings, £898.4m council dwellings) subject to new revaluation regime with limited auditor assurance
findings.detail: CIPFA Bulletin 22 requires full revaluation of land, buildings and surplus assets at 31 March 2026 (next full revaluation not due until 2030/31). Prior-year audit records 'a management-imposed limitation of scope over the valuations of the Council's land and buildings', meaning auditors did not obtain detailed evidence. Council dwellings of £898.4m are also subject to revaluation but are being handled separately.
findings.matters: These are the council's largest balance sheet items. A significant valuation error would overstate net worth. The auditor's note of a 'management-imposed limitation of scope' in prior year, combined with new revaluation requirements, suggests the council may struggle to defend valuations if challenged.
findings.figures: Land and buildings £833.7m; surplus assets £44.8m; council dwellings £898.4m
findings.quote: Given full revaluations will not be required again until 2030/31, with indexation applied in intervening years, it is even more important that valuations as at 31 March 2026 are appropriate and that the Council is able to support completion of audit procedures over these valuations.

findings.paper_title: Provisional Audit Planning Report , item 17.
findings.headline: Exceptional financial support received; financial position described as 'not as precarious' as prior year
findings.detail: Auditor notes that materiality was marginally increased because 'the Council's receipt of exceptional financial support means the Council's financial position is not as precarious in 2025/26 as it was during 2024/25.' This indicates the council has received government support to address a previous precarious financial position, and the materiality is set with that context in mind.
findings.matters: The council's financial position was described as precarious without exceptional support, and materiality is being set lower due to audit difficulties related to prior weakness in financial sustainability arrangements. This signals the council remains vulnerable to financial stress.
findings.figures: Materiality increased from 1.4% to 1.5% of gross expenditure (£15.4m) due to exceptional support
findings.quote: We have marginally increased our materiality from the 1.4% of gross expenditure on provision of services applied in 2024/25 as the Council's receipt of exceptional financial support means the Council's financial position is not as precarious in 2025/26 as it was during 2024/25.

findings.paper_title: Provisional Audit Planning Report , item 17.
findings.headline: Oracle Fusion implementation causing reconciliation failures and audit delays
findings.detail: Difficulties with Oracle Fusion migration are preventing timely reconciliations of key account balances. Auditor notes these reconciliation failures as a reason for incomplete procedures in 2024/25. Oracle system issues are blocking automation of bank reconciliation and wider balance sheet monitoring. GT has been commissioned for month 6 of 2025/26 to fix reconciliation processes and identify gaps, with target implementation from quarter 3 of 2025/26.
findings.matters: Failed reconciliations mean the council cannot reliably verify its own balance sheet month-to-month. This is a control failure that exposes the council to material misstatement and makes audit assurance difficult to build. It also signals IT/implementation risk.
findings.figures: Bank reconciliation process blocked; monthly/quarterly reconciliations targeted from 2026/27 financial year
findings.quote: It is our understanding that the difficulties experienced with the implementation of Oracle Fusion are a factor in why reconciliations were not performed as expected.

findings.paper_title: Provisional Audit Planning Report , item 17.
findings.headline: Auditor unable to form view on bad debt impairment (Collection Fund); high-risk account area unaudited
findings.detail: Auditors could not complete procedures on the council's non-domestic rates bad debt provisions for 2024/25 due to inability to arrange time with relevant officers to review complex models. The council significantly increased its impairment provision for 2024/25 but auditors have no evidence the assumptions are reasonable. Prior-year audit found impairment rates were not updated and were being applied to net debtors rather than gross balances.
findings.matters: Collection Fund debtors feed directly into council cash and borrowing headroom. If bad debt provisions are misstated, the council's liquidity position is overstated. Lenders need confidence in this figure; underprovision would hide cash stress.
findings.figures: Prior year finding: impairment percentages not updated for 2023/24; 2024/25 provision significantly increased but unaudited
findings.quote: We have been unable to complete our audit procedures over the Council's bad debt provisions as we were unable to arrange time with the relevant officers to obtain an understanding of these models. We have therefore been unable to form a view on whether the Council's revised bad debt provisions are reasonable.

findings.paper_title: Provisional Audit Planning Report , item 17.
findings.headline: Draft accounts delayed by nearly three months; statutory inspection period requirements not met
findings.detail: The 2024/25 draft Statement of Accounts was published 22 September 2025, nearly three months after the 1 July statutory deadline for commencement of public inspection. The council published a notice of delay but failed to explain the reasons as required by the Accounts and Audit Regulations 2015. This forced re-running of the inspection period and pushed the final audit backstop date.
findings.matters: Late accounts prevent lenders and council officers from accessing current financial information when needed. Non-compliance with statutory timelines suggests governance and project management failures beyond finance team capacity.
findings.figures: 22 September 2025 publication vs. 1 July 2025 deadline; three-month delay
findings.quote: The Council did not meet the statutory deadline for commencement of the public inspection period of its draft financial statements, and the inspection period it did run did not meet the requirements of the Accounts and Audit Regulations 2015.

findings.paper_title: Provisional Audit Planning Report , item 17.
findings.headline: Finance team capacity and information quality identified as significant weaknesses in value for money
findings.detail: Auditors have identified three significant weaknesses: capacity of the finance team is insufficient, quality of council information is poor, and financial sustainability is at risk. The 2024/25 audit revealed finance staff struggled with timeliness, were difficult to access, and could not provide data in formats auditors needed. Supporting working papers remain 'mixed' in quality; the council cannot reliably extract transaction-level data.
findings.matters: Finance team capacity directly affects the council's ability to manage borrowing covenants, produce timely reporting, and respond to financial stress. Poor information quality means neither the council nor lenders have reliable data on cash, receivables, or financial position.
findings.figures: 15 open recommendations from prior years, including Grade 1 (urgent) recommendations for reconciliations and bad debt impairment not yet satisfactorily addressed
findings.quote: The Council did not have proper arrangements in place to ensure the capacity of its finance team was sufficient to support the level of activity required of it.

findings.paper_title: Provisional Audit Planning Report , item 17.
findings.headline: Third consecutive disclaimer opinion expected despite recovery plan
findings.detail: The auditor expects to disclaim on the 2025/26 accounts due to 'pervasive gaps in assurance over opening balances, comparators and in-year movements', continuing a pattern from 2023/24 and 2024/25. The council is 'two years behind the illustrative timescale for the process of rebuilding assurance' and incomplete audit work in prior years means opening balances for 2025/26 cannot be properly verified.
findings.matters: A disclaimed opinion means auditors cannot state whether accounts are accurate. For lenders, this is uninsurable risk—they cannot rely on published financial statements to assess the council's true position or covenant compliance.
findings.figures: Disclaimer for 2023/24, 2024/25, and expected 2025/26; 'two years behind' recovery timeline
findings.quote: The audit report on the Council's 2025/26 financial statements will however need to be disclaimed due to the pervasive gaps in assurance over opening balances, comparators and in-year movements.

findings.paper_title: Internal Audit Annual Report for 2025-26 , item 19.
findings.headline: Significant reliance on finance business partners for budget forecasting with concerns about budget manager access to correct budget information
findings.detail: The Budget Delivery advisory review found budget awareness improved at manager level, but forecasting remains heavily dependent on finance staff and there are concerns about whether managers have access to accurate budget data.
findings.matters: Concentration of forecasting capability in finance teams rather than across budget holders indicates weak ownership and increases forecast unreliability
findings.quote: there was still significant reliance on finance business partners to set forecasts, and concerns about access to the correct budget information

findings.paper_title: Internal Audit Annual Report for 2025-26 , item 19.
findings.headline: Oracle financial system ongoing issues causing budget managers to abandon system and revert to informal Excel monitoring outside corporate systems
findings.detail: Multiple service audits found officers have lost confidence in the Oracle system due to persistent technical problems, reverting to spreadsheet-based monitoring outside the council's official financial management platform.
findings.matters: Loss of reliance on the corporate financial system undermines real-time budget visibility and creates audit trail gaps, increasing financial control risk
findings.quote: The ongoing issues with the Oracle system have impacted on budget managers' confidence in the system, with some reverting to excel monitoring arrangements outside the system as noted in the Highways and Greenspaces reviews.

findings.paper_title: Internal Audit Annual Report for 2025-26 , item 19.
findings.headline: Planned savings marked as unlikely to achieve in first quarter without identifying additional alternative savings
findings.detail: The Savings Programme review identified that planned savings for 2025/26 were at risk of not materialising without further intervention. New budget setting and savings monitoring processes were introduced mid-year, but effectiveness was not yet assessed at report date.
findings.matters: Inability to deliver planned savings signals revenue sustainability risk and questions the realism of future financial planning
findings.quote: the IA Savings Programme review noted many planned savings were marked as unlikely to be achieved within the first quarter without additional alternative savings identified

findings.paper_title: Internal Audit Annual Report for 2025-26 , item 19.
findings.headline: Council forecasted £36m overspend for 2025/26, with £21m from three service pressures: children's services £6.1m, adult social care £6.5m, and housing £8.3m
findings.detail: Budget monitoring identified significant service pressures early in the year. The IA found that the Savings Programme review noted many planned savings marked as unlikely to be achieved without additional alternative savings.
findings.matters: An overspend of this scale directly impacts council reserves and financial sustainability, signalling material budget control and delivery risks
findings.figures: £36m total overspend; £21m from services (children's £6.1m, adult social care £6.5m, housing £8.3m)
findings.quote: At the time of this report there is a forecasted £36m overspend against the agreed budget for 2025/26, with £21m due to service pressures in children's services (£6.1m), adult social care (£6.5m) and Housing (£8.3m).

findings.paper_title: Internal Audit Annual Report for 2025-26 , item 19.
findings.headline: Head of Internal Audit concluded Limited assurance opinion for 2025/26 due to significant control weaknesses still being remediated
findings.detail: The HIA opinion reflects an ongoing control environment with significant weaknesses in design and operation. While the council has taken steps to strengthen controls, governance processes are still embedding and not yet fully tested in practice.
findings.matters: A Limited assurance opinion signals material control environment risks that could affect financial reporting reliability and the council's ability to deliver objectives
findings.figures: 36% of assurance reviews received Limited opinions; 1 review received No Assurance
findings.quote: Although the HIA has concluded a Limited assurance opinion for 2025/26 they are optimistic we will see further improvements, and a reasonable assurance opinion is achievable if the current positive momentum is maintained.

findings.paper_title: Investment Strategy and Fund Manager Performance - Part 1
findings.paper_url: https://modgov.hillingdon.gov.uk/documents/s66726/6 Investment Strategy and Fund Manager Performance Update Part 1.pdf
findings.headline: Pension fund surplus declined by £21m in one quarter; liabilities rose £120m as discount rates fell and inflation assumptions increased
findings.detail: The pension fund's funding level decreased from 118% to 114% in the quarter to 31 March 2026. The surplus contracted from £211m to £190m while total liabilities increased by £120m, primarily due to lower discount rates and higher inflation assumptions applied by the fund's actuaries. Total fund assets declined from £1.58bn to £1.56bn, with £30m of the asset decline driven by market losses.
findings.matters: A deteriorating pension fund position and rising liabilities increase the risk of higher employer contribution rates being required to restore the fund to target funding. This directly affects the council's financial sustainability and the cash costs it must meet.
findings.figures: Funding level 118% to 114%; surplus £211m to £190m (£21m reduction); liabilities increased £120m; total assets £1.58bn to £1.56bn
findings.quote: Funding level decreased from 118% to 114%. Surplus reduced to £190m (£211m in Q4). Liabilities increased by £120m due to lower discount rates and higher inflation assumptions.

findings.paper_title: Investment Strategy Statement
findings.headline: Value at Risk increases £15m to £517m; modelled return improves only 0.3 percentage points (9.1% to 9.4%)
findings.detail: The strategy change is forecast to increase the modelled investment return from 9.1% to 9.4%—a gain of just 0.3 percentage points—while increasing Value at Risk from £502m to £517m. This represents a tradeoff in which the fund accepts meaningfully higher downside risk for marginal upside gain.
findings.matters: If actual returns fall short of the 9.4% assumption, or if markets turn sharply, the fund faces larger potential losses and could require the council to increase pension contributions to stabilize the fund.
findings.figures: Expected return increase 9.1% to 9.4% (+0.3 percentage points); VAR increase from £502m to £517m (+£15m)
findings.quote: The changes are forecast to increase the modelled investment return from 9.1% to 9.4% but with a small increase in the Value at Risk (VAR) from £502m to £517m.

findings.paper_title: Investment Strategy and Fund Manager Performance - Part I
findings.paper_url: https://modgov.hillingdon.gov.uk/documents/s66199/9 Investment Strategy and Fund Manager Performance Update Part 1.pdf
findings.headline: Pension fund liabilities increased by £230m following revaluation to 31 March 2025 assumptions, with the largest impact from a shift to more prudent discount rate assumptions
findings.detail: The funding level fell to 127% (from an implied ~146%), a 19% quarterly decline. The paper explains this step change is primarily driven by updating the valuation basis from March 2022 to March 2025 assumptions. The key driver is 'the biggest step change from the 2025 valuation is on the financial assumptions (i.e. the discount rate) as a result of the increased prudence level adopted compared to the previous valuation.' This reflects both real membership experience and more conservative measurement of liabilities.
findings.matters: Pension liabilities rank ahead of most unsecured creditors in any council financial stress, and more prudent liability assumptions typically signal pressure on future contribution budgets. A £230m increase materially affects the council's long-term financial position even though the funding level remains above 100%.
findings.figures: Funding level fell to 127% (19% quarterly decline); liabilities increased by £230m; assets at £1.58bn
findings.quote: The biggest step change from the 2025 valuation is on the financial assumptions (i.e. the discount rate) as a result of the increased prudence level adopted compared to the previous valuation.

findings.paper_title: 6a. London Borough of Hillingdon Pension Fund 2025 Funding Valuation Report - DRAFT , item 161.
findings.paper_url: https://modgov.hillingdon.gov.uk/documents/s66193/6a. London Borough of Hillingdon Pension Fund 2025 Funding Valuation Report - DRAFT.pdf
findings.headline: Climate change scenario analysis identifies a plausible downside pathway where Fund funding strategy would face material stress
findings.detail: The Fund modeled three climate change scenarios using narrative-driven analysis. Under the 'Climate Catastrophe' scenario (delayed action to climate change causing prolonged economic and social disruption), the likelihood of meeting funding targets falls below the Fund's required threshold for 10+ years. The report explicitly warns that this scenario is plausible and would stress the fund's strategy.
findings.matters: Climate change represents a tail risk to the fund's long-term viability and the council's finances; a delayed global response to climate risk could trigger contribution increases or asset write-downs affecting the council's financial flexibility
findings.figures: Base case stress test 79% likelihood of success; Climate Catastrophe scenario shows sustained period below Fund's required minimum likelihood; climate scenario assumes 20+ year impacts
findings.quote: There is therefore a plausible downside scenario prompted by a climate-related event that would put the Fund's funding strategy at risk

findings.paper_title: 6a. London Borough of Hillingdon Pension Fund 2025 Funding Valuation Report - DRAFT , item 161.
findings.paper_url: https://modgov.hillingdon.gov.uk/documents/s66193/6a. London Borough of Hillingdon Pension Fund 2025 Funding Valuation Report - DRAFT.pdf
findings.headline: Standardised peer comparison shows Fund 94% funded vs 118% on local assumptions, indicating local approach is significantly more optimistic than sector standard
findings.detail: The Fund reports 118% funding on its local assumptions but only 94% when measured using the standardised LGPS (SAB) basis required for peer comparison. The 24-percentage-point gap suggests the Fund's discount rate assumption (6.3%) is more optimistic than the sector standard, and the report notes the SAB basis is 'for comparison only' and does not drive contributions. However, the gap signals the council's improved contribution position may be more dependent on optimistic assumptions than the headline funding level suggests.
findings.matters: Indicates the council's pension obligation relief is contingent on achieving investment returns well above peer expectations, increasing the risk of reversals if markets or the fund's strategy underperform
findings.figures: Local funding level 118%; SAB standardised basis 94%; gap of 24 percentage points; SAB funding level decreased 4% since previous valuation
findings.quote: The Fund's SAB funding level at 31 March 2025 is 94%. SAB assumptions are to allow comparison only and are not intended to be appropriate for funding or setting contribution rates.

findings.paper_title: 6a. London Borough of Hillingdon Pension Fund 2025 Funding Valuation Report - DRAFT , item 161.
findings.paper_url: https://modgov.hillingdon.gov.uk/documents/s66193/6a. London Borough of Hillingdon Pension Fund 2025 Funding Valuation Report - DRAFT.pdf
findings.headline: Fund's funding position is highly sensitive to modest changes in inflation and returns assumptions, with limited margin for error
findings.detail: The report documents that if future inflation were only 0.1 percentage points higher than assumed, the funding level would fall by 2% (approximately £16m). Similarly, if salary growth exceeds assumptions by 0.5 percentage points, funding falls by 1% (£4m). The required annual investment return to achieve 100% funding has risen to 5.4% p.a. from 4.9% previously, indicating the fund is less resilient to market shocks.
findings.matters: The Fund's improved position has little buffer; small shortfalls in investment returns or overshoots in inflation or wage costs would quickly erode the surplus and likely trigger higher contribution demands
findings.figures: 0.1% higher inflation = 2% funding level reduction (c£16m fall); 0.5% higher salary growth = 1% funding level reduction (c£4m fall); required return to achieve 100% funding increased to 5.4% p.a. from 4.9% p.a.
findings.quote: Benefit increases: if future inflation was 0.1% pa higher than assumed at this valuation, then the funding level would reduce by around 2% (with a c£16m fall in the surplus).

findings.paper_title: 6a. London Borough of Hillingdon Pension Fund 2025 Funding Valuation Report - DRAFT , item 161.
findings.paper_url: https://modgov.hillingdon.gov.uk/documents/s66193/6a. London Borough of Hillingdon Pension Fund 2025 Funding Valuation Report - DRAFT.pdf
findings.headline: CPI inflation and salary growth significantly exceeded assumptions in the past three years, creating unfavorable variances of £167m and £15m respectively
findings.detail: Between 2022 and 2025, actual CPI inflation ran at 6.1% p.a. compared to the expected 2.7% p.a., with an unfavorable funding impact of £167m, and actual salary growth was 6.5% p.a. against expected 3.2%, costing £15m. The Fund's current assumptions for future inflation are 2.3% p.a. and for salary growth 2.8% p.a. The pattern of assumption misses in recent years suggests the current expectations may again prove optimistic.
findings.matters: Rising pension liabilities driven by higher-than-expected inflation and salary costs could emerge if economic conditions remain elevated, potentially triggering contribution increases when the fund is revalued in 2028
findings.figures: Benefit increases: expected 2.7% p.a., actual 6.1% p.a. (£167m negative impact); salary increases: expected 3.2% p.a., actual 6.5% p.a. (£15m negative impact); current assumptions 2.3% inflation, 2.8% salary growth
findings.quote: Investment returns 4.1% p.a. 2.9% p.a. (£53m); Benefit increases 2.7% p.a. 6.1% p.a. (£167m); Salary increases 3.2% p.a. 6.5% p.a. (£15m)

findings.paper_title: 6a. London Borough of Hillingdon Pension Fund 2025 Funding Valuation Report - DRAFT , item 161.
findings.paper_url: https://modgov.hillingdon.gov.uk/documents/s66193/6a. London Borough of Hillingdon Pension Fund 2025 Funding Valuation Report - DRAFT.pdf
findings.headline: Fund's improvement from deficit to 118% surplus is heavily dependent on increased investment return assumptions, despite recent underperformance
findings.detail: The funding level improved from 88% (deficit of £167m) to 118% (surplus of £211m), but the report explicitly states this improvement is 'primarily due to higher assumed future investment returns at 2025.' However, actual investment performance from 2022-2025 was 2.9% p.a. against the prior expectation of 4.1% p.a., costing the fund £53m. The continued improvements depend on whether future markets will meet the higher 6.3% annual return assumption.
findings.matters: The council's pension obligations may increase at the next valuation if investment returns do not meet the 6.3% assumption, potentially reversing the favorable contribution position, especially given recent market underperformance
findings.figures: Discount rate increased from 4.1% (2022) to 6.3% (2025); actual investment returns 2.9% p.a. vs expected 4.1% p.a.; funding level improved from 88% to 118%
findings.quote: The improvement in funding level is primarily due to higher assumed future investment returns at 2025.

findings.paper_title: 6a. London Borough of Hillingdon Pension Fund 2025 Funding Valuation Report - DRAFT , item 161.
findings.paper_url: https://modgov.hillingdon.gov.uk/documents/s66193/6a. London Borough of Hillingdon Pension Fund 2025 Funding Valuation Report - DRAFT.pdf
findings.headline: Employer contribution rates reduced to negative (secondary rate -0.5% for 2026/27 to 2028/29), improving cash position
findings.detail: The Fund's valuation sets employer contribution rates for the period 2026/27 to 2028/29. The secondary contribution rate has shifted from 4.1% annually in the previous valuation to negative -0.5%, meaning the Fund will credit the council approximately £1m per year rather than require additional contributions. The primary rate remains stable at 19.5% of pay.
findings.matters: Reduces the council's pension contribution obligations in the near term, improving cash flow and reducing financial stress during the period covered
findings.figures: Primary rate 19.5% (vs 19.6% previously); secondary rate 2026/27 -0.5% (vs 4.1% in 2023/24); monetary credits £1.028m (2026/27), £1.057m (2027/28), £1.087m (2028/29)
findings.quote: On average, employer total contribution rates (ie Primary plus Secondary) have reduced mainly due to higher assumed future investment returns at 2025 compared to 2022.

findings.paper_title: 260226 - 09 - 26-27 Budget - App 1 CFO S25 Statement , item 59.
findings.headline: Council's recent track record in savings delivery has been 'inconsistent', with under-delivered proposals rolled forward multiple times and inadequate implementation planning
findings.detail: CFO describes evidence of optimism bias in savings assumptions, weak implementation planning, unclear ownership, and undelivered savings carried forward into subsequent years sometimes multiple times. 2025/26 alone required £38.8m savings. CFO notes 'achieving a step change in delivery success will be essential', indicating past performance has been insufficient.
findings.matters: Savings are central mechanism for budget balance; past failures mean new savings carry material delivery risk; underperformance would force rapid reserve depletion and emergency measures
findings.figures: 2025/26 required £38.8m savings including £4.8m carried forward from 2024/25; high-value and high-risk proposals now require detailed delivery plans with Corporate Director sign-off
findings.quote: the Council's recent track record in savings delivery has been inconsistent. Achieving a step change in delivery success will be essential.

findings.paper_title: 260226 - 09 - 26-27 Budget - App 1 CFO S25 Statement , item 59.
findings.headline: Medium-term budget gap of £44.5m by 2028/29 remains unsolved despite improved funding settlement; CFO states this 'cannot be addressed through incremental savings alone'
findings.detail: Despite Fair Funding Review improvements, a £44.5m structural gap persists by 2028/29. Largest driver is continued temporary accommodation cost growth. CFO acknowledges this requires combination of major cost control, demand management, income maximisation and policy decisions. Additional £12.4m annual financing costs from EFS capitalisation compound the pressure.
findings.matters: Unsustainable medium-term position; likely to require further EFS, major service cuts, significant council tax rises or major policy changes; signals structural imbalance between income and demand
findings.figures: £44.5m gap 2028/29; £12.4m annual MRP and interest costs by 2028/29; temporary accommodation drives largest portion of gap
findings.quote: By the final year of the MTFS, the projected shortfall remains £44.5m, even after the full benefit of the phased funding reform has been incorporated.

findings.paper_title: 260226 - 09 - 26-27 Budget - App 1 CFO S25 Statement , item 59.
findings.headline: Temporary accommodation is single largest budget risk, with demand that 'does not correlate reliably' with demographics and is driven by economic factors outside council control
findings.detail: CFO explicitly warns that forecasting temporary accommodation carries 'inherent uncertainty despite improved modelling' because demand is driven by economic conditions, private rental market dynamics, asylum flows, and national policy changes. 5% inflation increase assumed for 2027/28 due to Renters Rights Act. Largest source of budget volatility.
findings.matters: Single largest uncontrollable cost driver; if demand exceeds forecast, depleted reserves will erode rapidly; housing market and asylum policy are outside council influence
findings.figures: TA volatility projects into years 2-3 of MTFS; 5% inflation increase assumed 2027/28; 2025/26 cost pressures from TA driven by market conditions and policy factors
findings.quote: temporary accommodation demand does not correlate reliably with demographic growth or other available indicators. Economic conditions, private sector rental market dynamics, asylum flows, and national policy changes all materially influence local demand.

findings.paper_title: 260226 - 09 - 26-27 Budget - App 1 CFO S25 Statement , item 59.
findings.headline: Internal Audit gave 'No Assurance' for 2024/25; external audit opinions disclaimed for three consecutive years with seven statutory recommendations
findings.detail: Internal Audit report identified 52% of assurance reviews as Limited or No Assurance, with weaknesses in asset management, contract management, and budget monitoring. External auditors unable to sign off accounts for three years. Seven statutory recommendations issued covering financial governance, budget realism, financial capacity, and medium-term planning.
findings.matters: Failed audit opinions signal fundamental control failures; auditors cannot provide assurance over financial statements; indicates risk of undetected issues and unreliable financial reporting
findings.figures: No Assurance opinion from Head of Internal Audit 2024/25; 3 consecutive years of disclaimed external audit opinions; 7 statutory recommendations; 52% of IA reviews Limited/No Assurance
findings.quote: The Internal Audit opinion for 2024/25 was 'No Assurance', external audit opinions have been disclaimed for three consecutive years

findings.paper_title: 260226 - 09 - 26-27 Budget - App 1 CFO S25 Statement , item 59.
findings.headline: General Fund Reserve depleted to £1.45m at March 2025, described as 'very significantly below' prudent levels for a council this size
findings.detail: Over 2022-2025, reserves declined at an average rate of £26.5m per year. CIPFA Resilience Index places the council at the high-risk end of comparator authorities for reserves, indicating loss of financial resilience through absorbing repeated overspends rather than structural overborrowing. Council now has zero buffer for cost pressures.
findings.matters: Lack of reserves means any deviation from budget immediately impacts financial stability; council cannot absorb demand shocks or unexpected costs
findings.figures: £26.5m average annual reserve decline 2022-2025; £1.45m GF reserve at March 2025; £24.2m reserve decline in 2024/25 alone
findings.quote: The General Fund Reserve reaching £1.45m at March 2025. This level is very significantly below what would normally be regarded as prudent for a council of Hillingdon's size and risk profile.

findings.paper_title: 260226 - 09 - 26-27 Budget - App 1 CFO S25 Statement , item 59.
findings.headline: Budget cannot balance without Exceptional Financial Support from government, which has not yet been formally confirmed
findings.detail: The CFO's entire opinion is predicated on confirmation of EFS for both 2025/26 and 2026/27. Without it, the council faced a £36m deficit and insolvent reserves. EFS is required to rebuild reserves to a working level of £41.5m and is described as central to the stabilisation strategy.
findings.matters: Lending decisions depend on solvency, which remains conditional on continued government support that may not be guaranteed beyond 2027
findings.figures: 2025/26 projected deficit £36m; General Fund reserve £1.45m at March 2025; projected position March 2026 would be -£34.5m without EFS
findings.quote: the confirmation by Government of Exceptional Financial Support for both 2025/26 and 2026/27, on terms sufficient to address the remaining forecast deficits and to enable the Council to stabilise and begin to rebuild its reserves

findings.detail: Multiple budget lines address DSG deficit reduction: Finance directorate's Enhanced Financial Capacity to Support DSG Deficit Reduction (£500k budgeted 2025/26, £192k spent), DSG Safety Valve (£4m budgeted, £0 spent), and DSG/SEND Improvement Plan (£2.4m budgeted, £353k spent). The paper provides no explanation for why such a large share of one of the council's major service areas' transformation investment did not proceed.

findings.headline: Transformation spending budgeted at £17m for 2025/26 but delivered only £5.7m, leaving £11.3m unspent
findings.detail: The council's transformation programme was budgeted at £17m but forecast spending only £5.7m, a 67% underspend. Multiple major projects did not proceed as planned: DSG Safety Valve (£4m budgeted, £0 spent), Corporate Services Transformation (£3.05m budgeted, £0 spent), and Financial Systems Improvement (£1.5m budgeted, £0 spent). The paper frames this as successful ROI because £5.7m delivered is forecasted to generate £9.9m in future benefits, but the scale of undelivered spend raises questions about programme management and delays.
findings.matters: A lender must assess whether the council has the capacity to deliver on transformation commitments; two-thirds of the planned transformation spend not happening suggests either programme delays or cancellations that could impact ability to realise planned savings.
findings.figures: Budget £17,000k, forecast outturn £5,669k, underspend £11,331k. Expected future financial benefit £9.9m from £5.7m investment.
findings.quote: This level of financial benefit is being achieved from a forecast capital transformation spend of £5.7m, against an originally approved transformation plan of £17m, demonstrating a strong return on investment.

findings.detail: Fair value of council's service company for housing delivery, in which it holds £3.4m shares, declined to £2.6m (31 March 2025) from prior year £4.2m. Valuation shift from projected future cash flows to actual recent-year cash flows suggests commercial returns are not materialising as originally forecast.
findings.matters: Declining valuation of flagship commercial investment suggests revenue-generation strategy through housing delivery is underperforming; limits council's ability to fund services through trading activity

findings.headline: Capital Financing Requirement forecast to grow 65% in two years to £972.4m, driving substantial increase in borrowing
findings.detail: CFR driven by capital investment programmes (water sports facility, school expansion, housing development, highways) plus £88m EFS capitalisation. Associated external debt forecast to reach £935.4m by 2026/27, increasing long-term revenue obligations through interest and MRP costs.
findings.matters: Rapid CFR growth indicates increasing long-term financial commitments and exposes council to refinancing risk as maturing loans must be replaced

findings.headline: Council requires £173m Exceptional Financial Support from government to offset 2025/26 overspend and restore depleted reserves
findings.detail: Hillingdon is in closing stages of agreeing EFS totalling £173m phased over 2025/26-2027/28 to address forecast revenue overspend, replenish General Fund and Earmarked Reserves, and enable balanced budget. EFS is delivered as capitalisation directive, effectively converting revenue costs to capital financed by borrowing, with the council required to provide MRP over 20 years.
findings.matters: Government financial support is a red flag for lenders, signalling the council cannot self-fund identified shortfalls and requires intervention

findings.headline: Business Rates safety net protection reduces from 100% in 2026/27 to 92.5% by 2028/29; risk of appeals on property revaluations not yet quantified.
findings.detail: The council is protected 100% against business rates income loss in 2026/27 but this reduces to 97% in 2027/28 and 92.5% in 2028/29. Government has implemented major business rates increases with significant revaluations that are being phased in (30%/25%/25% annual caps). There is material risk of appeals reducing income, which is not yet modelled in the MTFS.
findings.matters: The reducing safety net creates unquantified risk in later MTFS years. If appeals materialise as expected given the scale of revaluations, the council could face unexpected income loss at the precise time when EFS is being phased out and savings programme is at maximum strain.
findings.figures: 100% protection 2026/27; reduces to 97% in 2027/28 and 92.5% in 2028/29; property revaluations with 30%/25%/25% annual caps
findings.quote: The Council is protected in 2026/27 from any loss from appeals (i.e. a 100% safety net), but this protection reduces in 2027/28 to 97% and in 2028/29 to 92.5%... At this stage we have not made any adjustment to the MTFS

findings.paper_url: https://modgov.hillingdon.gov.uk/documents/s65768/2026-27 Budget and Medium Term Financial Strategy FINAL.pdf
findings.headline: EFS servicing costs (MRP and interest) will reach £12.5m per annum by 2028/29, permanently reducing resources available for service delivery.
findings.detail: The cumulative use of EFS (£88m in 2025/26, £62m in 2026/27, £23m in 2027/28) will incur revenue charges for Minimum Revenue Provision and interest. These costs are projected to reach £6.387m in 2026/27 and £12.467m by 2028/29. This is a permanent annual charge that cannot be avoided and reduces the council's capacity for service delivery.
findings.matters: Not only does the council need EFS to balance the budget now, but the cost of servicing that EFS will permanently consume resources. These costs actually increase during the MTFS period as the EFS stock accumulates.
findings.quote: the annual cost of servicing the MRP and interest on the cumulative EFS by 2028/29 would amount to £12.5m per annum

findings.paper_title: 2026/27 Budget and Future Medium-Term Financial Strategy (to recommend to Council)
findings.paper_url: https://modgov.hillingdon.gov.uk/documents/s65768/2026-27 Budget and Medium Term Financial Strategy FINAL.pdf
findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant (DSG) deficit of £75.5m; statutory override ends March 2028, after which council must bear residual deficit from own resources.
findings.detail: The cumulative DSG deficit is forecast at £75.5m at 31 March 2026, rising to £87.9m before government support. The statutory override that keeps this separate from General Fund reserves ends 31 March 2028. While government announced a 90% grant to cover accrued deficits up to 2025/26, the council estimates it will need to set aside approximately £6m to cover the residual deficit from 2028/29 onwards.
findings.matters: When the override ends, the council must either absorb the deficit impact into General Fund or maintain very high reserves specifically for this purpose. This is an identified future call on finances at a time when EFS is being phased out.
findings.figures: £75.5m deficit at 31 March 2026; estimated £6m residual deficit to be borne by council from 2028/29; 90% grant expected autumn 2026
findings.quote: the cumulative deficit carried forward at 31 March 2026 is forecast at £75.5m... The Statutory Override will end on 31 March 2028. Therefore, local authorities will need to plan to be able to meet the cost of the residual deficit from their own resources in 2028/29

findings.headline: Housing Revenue Account (HRA) debt-to-income ratio at maximum sustainable level of 5:1; severely limits future borrowing capacity.
findings.detail: The HRA Capital Financing Requirement is rising from £354.5m in 2025/26 to £524.7m by 2030/31. The council notes that the debt-to-income ratio 'meets the recommended limit of 5:1 throughout the planning period'. This is the maximum sustainable level, leaving no headroom for additional borrowing.
findings.matters: The HRA manages 10,200 social housing units and generates £77.6m annual rental income. Being at the borrowing ceiling means any further housing investment, service improvements, or regulatory costs would require either revenue contribution increases (pressuring rents) or additional General Fund support.
findings.figures: HRA CFR £354.5m rising to £524.7m; debt-to-income ratio 5:1 (at maximum sustainable limit); HRA income £77.6m

findings.headline: £44.5m budget gap remains unfunded by 2028/29 despite proposed savings of £29.2m; no plan identifies where further savings would come from.
findings.detail: Even after the council delivers £29.2m of savings over three years, a £44.5m gap persists. The MTFS assumes 'further efficiencies or savings for 2027/28 and 2028/29 will be found before the start of those latter years' but does not specify what these are or how they will be achieved. The paper notes that 'difficult decisions will need to be made in the coming years'.
findings.matters: The council's three-year plan is not balanced and depends on finding unidentified savings of approximately 15% of General Fund expenditure, implying structural imbalance.

findings.paper_title: 2026/27 Budget and Future Medium-Term Financial Strategy (to recommend to Council)
findings.paper_url: https://modgov.hillingdon.gov.uk/documents/s65768/2026-27 Budget and Medium Term Financial Strategy FINAL.pdf
findings.headline: Hillingdon losing £65m in government funding due to phased Fair Funding Review implementation; historic damping penalty continues since 2013/14.
findings.detail: Government has finally recognised Hillingdon's funding needs through the Fair Funding Review, but implementation is phased over three years, not immediate. The council will not receive the full assessed amount until 2028/29, meaning it loses £65m in funding during 2026/27 and 2027/28. Additionally, Hillingdon was hit with a £4.8m negative damping grant in 2013/14 to support other councils, and continues to face damping penalties.
findings.matters: A lender would note that the council is being systematically underfunded against government's own need assessment, and that relief is delayed. The council is forced to bridge this timing gap using EFS.
findings.figures: £65m lost funding during 2026/27-2027/28 combined; £4.8m historic damping penalty from 2013/14
findings.quote: Our analysis of the data set out in the LGFS indicates that Hillingdon will lose £65m in funding that Government calculates Hillingdon needs, in order to support and slow down the reductions faced by other Councils... the council's EFS requirement is more than had it received the full calculation from 2026/27

findings.headline: Temporary Accommodation pressure of £1.652m in 2026/27 alone, with further £6.576m over next two years; demand fundamentally unpredictable.
findings.detail: The council revised temporary accommodation budgets after initial December proposals, identifying a net pressure of £1.652m in 2026/27 and a further £6.576m over the following two years. The paper notes that 'the projections in this service area are less predictable as there is no correlation with population growth or other clear demographic indicators that provide reliable trend analysis'.
findings.matters: Temporary accommodation is a statutory obligation. Unpredictable demand that cannot be modelled creates a hidden budget risk that could force mid-year adjustments or require additional reserves when the council is already depleted.
findings.figures: £1.652m pressure in 2026/27; £6.576m additional over 2027/28-2028/29
findings.quote: the projections in this service area are less predictable as there is no correlation with population growth or other clear demographic indicators that provide reliable trend analysis

findings.headline: General Fund reserves depleted to £1.45m at March 2025; council requesting £40m of EFS just to rebuild to acceptable range.
findings.detail: General Fund reserves have been drawn down over years to bridge funding gaps. The £40m rebuild portion of the £88m EFS request represents 45% of the 2025/26 ask, leaving only £12m for other pressures and risks.
findings.matters: Dangerously low reserves indicate the council has exhausted its financial shock absorbers and has limited headroom for unforeseen pressures. The council is explicitly requesting government support just to reach acceptable reserve levels.

findings.paper_title: 2026/27 Budget and Future Medium-Term Financial Strategy (to recommend to Council)
findings.paper_url: https://modgov.hillingdon.gov.uk/documents/s65768/2026-27 Budget and Medium Term Financial Strategy FINAL.pdf
findings.headline: Budget cannot be set without Exceptional Financial Support (EFS) — effectively deficit financing requiring government approval.
findings.detail: The council faces a £61.4m budget gap in 2026/27 and cannot legally balance its budget without government support. EFS of £62m has been requested for 2026/27, and an additional £88m for 2025/26 (cumulative £150m). At the time of writing, MHCLG had not yet confirmed this support, meaning Cabinet could not definitively approve a balanced budget.
findings.matters: A lender would need to understand that the council's budget position is unsustainable without ongoing government intervention, and that confirmation of support was outstanding when this paper was written. This is structural reliance on central support, not a one-off event.
findings.figures: £61.4m gap in 2026/27; £62m EFS requested for 2026/27; £88m EFS for 2025/26; cumulative ask of £150m
findings.quote: It is not possible for the Council to set a legally balanced budget in 2026/27 without the use of EFS, hence this budget is constructed on the explicit assumption that it is subject to an in-principle agreement from MHCLG

findings.paper_title: Appendix 3 - Audit Results Report , item 188.
findings.headline: Pension fund liability of £183 million — material balance sheet risk
findings.detail: The Council's defined benefit pension fund deficit totalled £183 million at 31 March 2024. While the auditor concluded 2024/25 pension balances appear reasonable, they noted an immaterial understatement of £2.5 million in pension assets from misstatements in the pension fund's valuations, and flagged ongoing uncertainty about application of the 'Virgin Media v NTL' legal case to the Local Government Pension Scheme.
findings.matters: A £183 million pension liability is a major unfunded obligation on the Council's balance sheet, representing long-term cost pressure that cannot be avoided.
findings.figures: Pension fund deficit: £183 million (as at 31 March 2024); misstatement identified: £2.5 million understatement of assets
findings.quote: The Council's pension fund deficit is a material estimated balance and the CIPFA Code requires that this liability be disclosed on the Council's balance sheet. At 31 March 2024, this totalled £183 million

findings.paper_title: Appendix 3 - Audit Results Report , item 188.
findings.headline: Audit identified £11.7 million in misstatements; adjusted adjustments reduce reserves by £3.3 million
findings.detail: The audit identified multiple material misstatements including: £11.7 million misclassification of borrowings; £5.6 million from incorrect revaluation of council dwellings; £1.5 million from school bank account items; £1.3 million from incorrect posting of rent rebates; and £1.3 million from omitted housing benefit. Management agreed to correct known adjustments (reducing reserves by £3.3 million) but left uncorrected adjustments of £0.1 million.
findings.matters: Multiple material errors in the financial statements indicate weak financial controls and careless record-keeping, undermining confidence in reported numbers.
findings.figures: Corrected misstatements: £11.7 million total; impact on reserves: £3.3 million reduction; uncorrected: £0.1 million
findings.quote: The impact of corrected audit differences was to reduce the Council's reserves by £3.3 million and remaining uncorrected audit differences would further decrease reserves by £0.1 million. These amounts, whilst not material, are significant in the context of the Council's limited reserves balance at 31 March 2025

findings.paper_title: Appendix 3 - Audit Results Report , item 188.
findings.headline: Four Section 151 Officers (chief finance officers) within 12 months; two departed without notice
findings.detail: The Council had four different Section 151 Officers between March 2024 and April 2025. The original permanent Section 151 Officer left in August 2024 without working notice; the interim replacement left in April 2025 also without notice. Both received payments in lieu of notice (three months' salary). The permanent officer also received an ex-gratia payment of a further three months' salary.
findings.matters: Rapid turnover of the Council's chief finance officer signals instability at the top of financial management and suggests the role is untenable, likely due to the financial crisis and governance pressures.
findings.figures: Four Section 151 Officers in 12 months; two early departures with payments in lieu; permanent officer also received ex-gratia payment
findings.quote: The Council has had four Section 151 Officers within a period of little more than 12 months... Both the former permanent Section 151 Officer and Interim Section 151 Officer left the Council without working a notice period, and received contractual payments equivalent to three months' salary as payment in lieu of notice. In addition, the former permanent Section 151 Officer received an additional negotiated ex-gratia payment equivalent to a further three months' salary

findings.paper_title: Appendix 3 - Audit Results Report , item 188.
findings.headline: Council has applied to MHCLG for exceptional financial support (outcome still awaited)
findings.detail: The Council forecast in July 2025 that it would not have sufficient reserves to support itself through to the end of 2025/26 and applied to the Ministry for Housing, Communities and Local Government for exceptional financial support. As of the audit report date (3 February 2026), the Council was still awaiting MHCLG's response.
findings.matters: An application for exceptional support is a public acknowledgement of near-insolvency. If MHCLG refuses, the Council will need emergency statutory intervention or forced savings.
findings.figures: Application made following July 2025 forecast of insufficient reserves through end of 2025/26
findings.quote: The Council forecast as early as July 2025, based on its assessment of its financial position as at 31 May 2025, that the Council would not have sufficient reserves to support itself through to the end of the 2025/26 financial year and sought exceptional financial support from MHCLG

findings.paper_title: Appendix 3 - Audit Results Report , item 188.
findings.headline: 2025/26 budget showing significant overspends by period 2 and questioned for compliance with balanced budget duty
findings.detail: Significant overspends are emerging against the 2025/26 budget as early as period 2 (by October 2025), coupled with the Council having assumed higher reserves than actually exist. The Section 151 Officer flagged concerns in their own budget report, and auditors concluded they cannot verify the Council met its statutory duty to set a balanced budget.
findings.matters: This indicates the Council is not living within its spending power and is already in distress in the current year. Non-compliance with the statutory duty to set a balanced budget is a formal governance failure.
findings.figures: Significant overspends emerging by period 2 of 2025/26; Section 151 Officer concerns flagged in their own Section 25 report
findings.quote: The emergence of significant overspends against the Council's 2025/26 budget, set during 2024/25, as early as period 2 of the 2025/26 financial year, coupled with much lower actual reserves as at 31 March 2025 than the Council had assumed in setting its 2025/26 budget together raise questions over the reliability of the Council's 2025/26 budget. These concerns were highlighted by the Council's Section 151 Officer themselves in their Section 25 report on the 2025/26 budget, and leave us unable to conclude that the Council is compliant with its statutory duty to set a balanced budget in respect of the 2025/26 financial year

findings.paper_title: Appendix 3 - Audit Results Report , item 188.
findings.headline: DSG (schools) deficit of £65.6 million — nearly 10 times remaining reserves
findings.detail: The Dedicated Schools Grant deficit grew by £18.1 million in 2024/25 to reach £65.6 million cumulatively. This is an accumulated overspend on schools funding that the Council must eventually repay from general reserves, but the Council has no credible plan to balance the schools budget until 2027/28.
findings.matters: This liability is nearly 10 times the Council's remaining reserves. If forced to repay it quickly, the Council would be insolvent. It represents unsustainable structural demand exceeding funding.
findings.figures: Cumulative DSG deficit: £65.6 million; Year-on-year increase 2024/25: £18.1 million; Plan to balance: 2027/28
findings.quote: The Council's Dedicated Schools Grant (DSG) deficit increased by £18.1 million during 2024/25, to a cumulative deficit of £65.6 million. This balance is almost ten times the remaining reserves of the Council, and is likely to continue to increase as the Council does not have plans to balance its schools budget until 2027/28

findings.paper_title: Appendix 3 - Audit Results Report , item 188.
findings.headline: Council recorded £31.5 million overspend (11.1% of budget) in 2024/25
findings.detail: The Council overspent its budget by £31.5 million comprising £17.4 million of planned budget overspend and £14.1 million of one-off accounting adjustments from a balance sheet review. This demonstrates inability to control spending within budget.
findings.matters: An 11% budget overspend signals fundamental problems with financial control, planning, and the Council's ability to live within its means.
findings.figures: Total overspend £31.5 million (11.1% of net budget): £17.4 million planned overspend + £14.1 million one-off impacts
findings.quote: The Council reported a significant overspend of £31.5 million (11.1% of its net budget) for 2024/25. This consisted of a £17.4 million overspend against the planned budget for 2024/25 and £14.1 million of one-off impacts arising from a balance sheet review

findings.paper_title: Appendix 3 - Audit Results Report , item 188.
findings.headline: Reserves depleted to only 20.9% of minimum required level
findings.detail: The Council's available reserves at 31 March 2025 were just £6.7 million, representing only 20.9% of the minimum level of reserves determined as necessary by the Section 151 Officer. This represents a critically low buffer for a major local authority.
findings.matters: Reserves are the Council's financial shock absorber; at this level, any unexpected cost or revenue shortfall could trigger a funding crisis.
findings.figures: Available reserves: £6.7 million; Minimum required: £32 million
findings.quote: The closing reserves of the Council at 31 March 2025 were just £6.7 million, which represents only 20.9% of the minimum level of reserves determined as necessary by the Council's Section 151 Officer

findings.paper_title: Appendix 3 - Audit Results Report , item 188.
findings.headline: Council will receive disclaimed audit opinion on 2024/25 financial statements
findings.detail: The auditor has not been able to complete all planned audit procedures and has not obtained sufficient evidence to conclude the financial statements are free from material misstatement. This follows a disclaimed opinion on 2023/24 statements. The delays stem from the Council publishing its draft accounts nearly three months late (22 September vs 1 July deadline) and providing incomplete working papers.
findings.matters: A disclaimed opinion means the Council's financial position cannot be audited or verified, which is a major red flag for any lender considering credit decisions.
findings.figures: Draft Statement of Accounts published 22 September 2025, nearly three months after statutory deadline of 1 July 2025
findings.quote: We have not been able to complete our planned programme of work to obtain sufficient evidence to have reasonable assurance over all closing balances

findings.paper_title: Appendix 5 - Pension Fund Audit results report , item 188.
findings.headline: The Council's auditors have reported a significant weakness in value for money relating to the Oracle Fusion finance system implementation.
findings.detail: The Council migrated to Oracle Fusion in May 2024, separating combined records for four entities (Council, Pension Fund, Hillingdon First Limited, Mayor's Charitable Trust) that had previously been in the same general ledger. The Council's auditors identified significant weaknesses in arrangements to secure value for money in this implementation.
findings.matters: Significant weaknesses in the Council's core finance system implementation raise questions about management's ability to execute major IT projects and maintain reliable financial controls across all Council operations.
findings.figures: Oracle Fusion live date: May 2024; contains records for four separate entities
findings.quote: The Council's auditors have reported a significant weakness in the Council's arrangements to secure value for money in relation to the implementation of Oracle Fusion.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 5 - Pension Fund Audit results report , item 188.
findings.headline: A newly identified moderate-risk control deficiency: inconsistent treatment of distributions between custodian and fund manager.
findings.detail: Income distributions are incorrectly classified as capital distributions and vice versa. These misclassifications lead to discrepancies in investment income recognition. The Pension Fund relies on custodian reporting as its primary source, making these errors significant. Management has been asked to strengthen diligence in reviewing custodian treatment.
findings.matters: Custodian control deficiencies increase the risk that investment values are misstated, affecting both pension fund valuations and the Council's liability assessments.
findings.figures: Newly identified in 2024/25 audit, rated as Moderate risk
findings.quote: We noted inconsistencies in the treatment of distributions by the custodian compared to the fund manager. Specifically, income distributions were incorrectly classified as capital distributions, and vice versa.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 5 - Pension Fund Audit results report , item 188.
findings.headline: The same investment income classification error in the LCIV Mac fund has now been identified for three consecutive years (2022/23, 2023/24, 2024/25).
findings.detail: Distributions reinvested at year end are not properly communicated by the fund manager or identified by the custodian, causing income to be understated. The auditors identified this as a control deficiency in addition to the accounting error. The amounts involved were £4.2 million in 2022/23 and £3.4 million in 2023/24; a similar issue with AEW UK Urban Real Estate has been identified this year.
findings.matters: Recurring seven-figure errors across three years indicate persistent control weaknesses that affect the accuracy of the Council's financial reporting on investment income.
findings.figures: £4.2 million in 2022/23, £3.4 million in 2023/24
findings.quote: In both the 2023/24 and 2022/23 audits we have identified the same error in relation to income from the LCIV Mac fund. Distributions from this fund are reinvested at year end and, in both years, this was not communicated by the fund manager nor identified by the custodian.

findings.paper_title: Appendix C - General Fund: Capital Programme , item 5.
findings.headline: Capital spending is heavily front-loaded in 2026/27 and 2027/28, with 55% of the 5-year programme in the first two years
findings.detail: Planned spend is £74.8m (2026/27), £48.9m (2027/28), then declining to £44.6m, £34.6m, and £25.9m in subsequent years. This concentration means borrowing obligations and debt service start immediately, placing near-term pressure on revenue resources.
findings.matters: Front-loaded capital programmes create earlier debt-service obligations, affecting current revenue sufficiency and financial flexibility during the critical first two years.
findings.figures: 2026/27: £74.838m (32.7% of 5-year total); first two years: £123.719m (54.1% of total)

findings.paper_title: Appendix C - General Fund: Capital Programme , item 5.
findings.headline: 46.4% of the capital programme (£106.2m) depends on external grants and contributions not fully controlled by the council
findings.detail: The capital programme relies on £106.2m from external sources including existing grants and contributions. Entire projects such as the £21.7m Hillingdon Water Sports Facility are entirely grant-dependent. Programme delivery and scope are at risk if external funding does not materialise, requiring either programme reduction or additional borrowing.
findings.matters: External funding is not guaranteed and shortfalls would create funding gaps that must be closed by either reducing capital investment or increased borrowing.
findings.figures: £106.174m external funding (46.4% of 5-year total); £31.519m existing grants & contributions in 2026/27; Water Sports Facility £21.706m (fully grant-dependent)

findings.paper_title: Appendix C - General Fund: Capital Programme , item 5.
findings.headline: Council committing to £122.6m prudential borrowing to finance 53.6% of its £228.8m 5-year capital programme
findings.detail: The General Fund capital programme totals £228.8m from 2026/27 to 2030/31, with £122.6m financed through prudential borrowing. The highest spend is in 2026/27 at £74.8m, of which £40.9m (54.6%) is from borrowing. Major borrowing items include SEND Meadow High School (£8.6m fully borrowed), Civic Centre Transformation (£3.5m fully borrowed), and School Building Condition Works (£9.2m).
findings.matters: The scale of borrowing directly determines future debt-service charges against revenue and is central to assessing debt sustainability and credit risk.
findings.figures: £122.618m total 5-year borrowing (53.6% of programme); £40.866m borrowing in 2026/27 (54.6% of that year's spend)

findings.paper_title: Appendix E – Housing Revenue Account: Capital Programme , item 5.
findings.paper_url: https://modgov.hillingdon.gov.uk/documents/s65359/Appendix E Housing Revenue Account Capital Programme.pdf
findings.headline: HRA is deploying £50m in year one for housing supply acquisitions, funded by £30m borrowing.
findings.detail: A major new acquisitions programme has been launched with £50m invested in 2026/27 alone under 'HRA In-House Housing Supply Acquisitions', using £30m of borrowing and £20m from other sources. This appears to represent a strategic shift toward acquiring homes rather than relying solely on building.
findings.matters: This signals a material change in HRA strategy and appetite for asset acquisition. A lender would want to understand the acquisitional asset quality, the borrowing terms, and whether this is a one-off investment or an ongoing commitment that might limit future HRA headroom.
findings.figures: £50m in year one, £30m borrowing, £20m other funding

findings.paper_title: Appendix E – Housing Revenue Account: Capital Programme , item 5.
findings.paper_url: https://modgov.hillingdon.gov.uk/documents/s65359/Appendix E Housing Revenue Account Capital Programme.pdf
findings.headline: Hayes Regeneration programme (£212.5m) is heavily concentrated in years 2–3, with £125m borrowing.
findings.detail: The largest single capital scheme is Hayes Regeneration across two phases totalling £212.48m. Spending peaks in 2027/28 (£79.812m) and 2028/29 (£87.962m), with the majority of the £125.248m borrowing required in those years. This concentration creates cash flow and affordability risk if rental income does not keep pace.
findings.matters: A lender would be concerned about concentration risk — if the HRA cannot generate sufficient surplus in those peak years, it may need to draw reserves or reduce maintenance spending. The timing also matters for debt service planning.
findings.figures: £212.480m over five years, £79.812m (year 2), £87.962m (year 3), £125.248m borrowing

findings.headline: Hillingdon's HRA plans to borrow £268m over five years to fund a £522m capital programme.
findings.detail: The capital programme runs 2026/27 to 2030/31 with total expenditure of £522.192m. Borrowing covers £268.193m (51%), with the remainder from revenue contributions, Right to Buy receipts, and grants. This represents a substantial increase in HRA debt that will require sustained rental income to service.
findings.matters: HRA borrowing directly increases the council's overall debt position and affects its ability to borrow for other services. A lender would want to understand the scale of this commitment and whether HRA rental income can sustain the debt service.
findings.figures: £522.192m total expenditure, £268.193m borrowing, £253.999m other funding over five years

news_drafts.headline: Hillingdon on course with savings plan but faces emerging demand pressures
news_drafts.lead: Hillingdon Council has delivered £13.1m of its £27.1m planned savings for 2026/27, with a further £7.9m on track for completion, putting 77% of the programme within reach. However, emerging demand pressures threaten the forecast. The number of households placed by the council in temporary nightly accommodation increased by 11 in the first four months against a budgeted reduction of 7, and the council has identified a £1.2m risk if the trend continues. The schools budget faces a £13.1m overspend on support for children with special educational needs, driven by parents applying before government reforms take effect, though this has been set aside in reserves under temporary government rules. Capital investment fell £31.7m behind forecast, deferring major projects including school building condition works and care home capacity into future years.

news_drafts.headline: Hillingdon on track to deliver three-quarters of cost-cutting plan by mid-year
news_drafts.lead: Hillingdon Council has delivered nearly half its planned £27m savings programme and has another 29 per cent on track, leaving three-quarters of the cuts and efficiency gains secured by Month 4 of the financial year. The council committed to the savings plan to balance its budget. Of the remaining quarter, 14 per cent is at risk of not delivering as planned, mostly from schemes to sell land and houses that require active management, and 2 per cent is unable to be delivered and will need alternative solutions. The shortfalls are not yet large enough to threaten the overall financial plan. The council also faces discrete pressures: a £13.1m overspend on support for children with special educational needs, a rise in homelessness demand despite fewer households in temporary accommodation at year-start, and cost inflation in passenger transport and waste. These are being watched but have not derailed the budget so far.

news_drafts.headline: Hillingdon delays a quarter of planned capital investment
news_drafts.lead: Hillingdon Council is pushing back £31.7m of its planned £126m capital spending, delaying a quarter of the investment programme to 2027-28 and beyond. The slippage affects major services including school building condition works (£10.8m), care home capacity projects (£7.5m) and disabled facilities grants (£4.4m). According to the council's budget monitoring, £17.2m of the planned £94.5m spend has not yet commenced or remains at planning stage. The deferred money will be spent in later years, reducing the council's borrowing needs for this financial year.
